tasks.short: Turn board budget rules into policies the three sites can follow.

today.trigger: The Finance Director or the board issues a budget directive after the budget round or a mid-year correction: a cost ceiling, a flex cap, a margin floor, or a pause on hiring.
steps: Read the directive in Outlook or the SharePoint budget pack, then the policy that is already in force.
Map it onto AFAS cost centres, the Rotterdam, Tilburg and Venlo sites, and labour types: own staff, overtime, and agency flex.
Check it against the transport CAO, the warehouse CAO, and any works-council agreement already in force.
Write the carrying-out rules: who may spend, what needs a request, and what is blocked.
Walk the Controller and the site leads through the exceptions, then file the policy on SharePoint.
drudgery: Re-reading last year's policy to see which lines still apply.
Copying the same rule into a separate version for each site.
Chasing which AFAS cost centre a sentence in the board pack actually hits.
today.time_sinks: Most of the time goes into matching the written directive to the way the three sites already book costs in AFAS, then rewriting the same rule so each site will follow it.

lenses.faster: Reading the old policy, mapping the directive onto cost centres, and writing the first draft drop out of the hand work. Deciding what the board meant, and what the sites will follow, stays with the analyst.
lenses.autonomous: When a signed directive is filed in the Finance SharePoint library, a draft policy and a list of clashes with current AFAS bookings are ready the next morning.
lenses.ambitious: At a tenth of the effort, Noordhaven would keep a living rule per site and cost type, updated with every directive, and would check each month whether the bookings still match it.
lenses.joy: Re-reading last year's PDF and making three near-copies is work nobody will miss. The part worth keeping is the talk with the Controller and the site leads about the real exceptions.
lenses.options: The same directive comes back as several workable policies: a tight cap, a practical cap with a peak-season exception, and a version per site, each showing which bookings would fail.
lenses.altitude: The analyst stops drafting each policy from a blank page and keeps the checklist every new directive must pass: CAO, works council, cost centre, owner, and expiry.
reach: The Controller's budget-manual updates and the coding notes the bookkeepers use on agency invoices.
The HR Business Partner's flex-cap note before a peak-season order goes to the agencies.
The Accountant's check of which costs a new rule pushes into another period.

tasks.human_edge: The analyst can tell what a vague board sentence was meant to stop, and which of Rotterdam, Tilburg or Venlo will quietly work around a rule that ignores the peak season.
tasks.pattern_why: The directive arrives as prose, and the policy has to survive the CAO and the works council. The analyst stays the author; the model prepares the draft, the cost-centre map, and the clash list.

in_practice.trigger: A new or revised budget directive is saved to the Finance SharePoint library or sent by the Finance Director.
steps: Pull the directive, the current policy, the CAO notes on overtime and allowances, and the open works-council agreements.
Map each line to AFAS cost centres, sites, and labour types, and flag bookings that would break it.
Draft the policy: limits, approver, exceptions, start date, and aggregation so no individual's pay is shown.
Write a one-pager per site and a short note on any point that needs works-council advice or consent under the WOR.
The analyst edits the draft and the Finance Director approves it before it is published.
in_practice.human_gate: The Finance Director approves the policy before it is published. If it changes working time, staffing, or a scheme the works council has rights on, that route is finished before the sites are bound.
data_needed: CAO clauses on overtime and allowances
Last twelve months of actuals by cost centre and labour type
in_practice.logs_to: The SharePoint policy library, with version, author, approver, and a short decision note the Controller can cite at close.

evidence.claim: Workday Adaptive Planning stores budget assumptions, approval limits, and scenarios as versioned data, which is the same job as turning a directive into a rule a plan can apply.
evidence.source: Workday Adaptive Planning; model knowledge of product scope

evidence.claim: AFAS Profit holds cost centres, budgets, and workflows, so a decided limit can sit in the finance system the bookkeepers already post to.
evidence.source: AFAS Profit; model knowledge of product scope

evidence.claim: Drafting a policy from a directive plus last year's text is ordinary document work, and a person still has to judge CAO and works-council points.
A shift change, a cap on hours, or a change in how warehouse work is organised can fall under the works council's advice or consent rights in the WOR.

risks: A clean draft gets published before works-council advice or consent, and the sites are then told to ignore it.
A vague board sentence becomes a hard cap and blocks legitimate peak-season flex in Venlo or Tilburg.
Cost-centre names in the directive do not match AFAS, so the policy governs the wrong bookings.
A site one-pager shows individual pay or absence detail, which conflicts with the AVG.
research_questions: Which budget directives in the last two years actually changed how the sites booked costs, and which were ignored?
Do any current directives touch working time, overtime, or flex volume in a way that needs works-council advice or consent?
How often do the cost-centre names in the board pack differ from the names in AFAS?
Does AFAS already enforce spending limits that a written policy would only repeat?

tasks.short: Run the numbers on a request and show which option pays back.

today.trigger: A site manager, the Finance Director, or the Controller asks for a comparison: a shift pattern, more agency hours, racking, a truck lease, or a thin-margin customer contract.
steps: Collect the request from mail and the numbers from AFAS, the agency portals, and any Rabobank lease or loan quote.
Rebuild the case in Excel because last quarter's file does not fit this request.
Add labour cost with CAO rates, overtime, and the agency premium, plus a volume assumption from the site.
Run one base case, write the memo, and send it back.
Rework the file when the Controller challenges the volume or the rate.
drudgery: Rebuilding the same Excel structure for every request.
Hunting agency rates and CAO premiums that the request left out.
Retyping actuals from AFAS or Power BI into the model.
today.time_sinks: The hours go to finding comparable actuals and rebuilding the spreadsheet. A request often waits days because the analyst is on the close, and then it is reworked once the assumptions are questioned.

lenses.faster: Pulling actuals, loading CAO and agency rates, and building the base, downside, and upside cases drop out of the copy-and-paste. The call on the volume assumption stays.
lenses.autonomous: A request on a short form starts the model run on the latest AFAS extract, and the pack is waiting for review without a chase mail.
lenses.ambitious: At a tenth of the effort, every site request above a set amount would get a full case before money is committed, including the small ones that now go through on a mail thread.
lenses.joy: Rebuilding the workbook and chasing rate cards is work nobody will miss. What remains is the argument about the few assumptions that change the answer.
lenses.options: Each request comes back as a small set of cases: base, volume down, rate up, lease versus buy, and own hours versus agency, with payback and cash in the same layout.
lenses.altitude: The analyst stops being the spreadsheet engine and owns the standard case layout, the rate sources, and the test that a case is complete before it reaches the Controller.
reach: The Accountant's lease-versus-buy working and the fixed-asset treatment that follows it.
The Credit and Collections Officer's check on whether a thin-margin customer also pays late.
The HR Business Partner's cost comparison of a fixed contract against agency flex.

tasks.human_edge: The analyst can tell which volume and service assumptions are wishful, and whether a saving on paper breaks the CAO, the shift pattern, or a promise already made to a customer.
tasks.pattern_why: The actuals, rate cards, and arithmetic can be fetched and checked, and the request itself is unstructured. A case that moves money or headcount counts only after the analyst, and above a threshold the Controller, accepts the assumptions.

in_practice.trigger: A financial request arrives on a short form, or is forwarded by the Finance Director, with purpose, site, amount, timing, and expected volume.
steps: Load trailing actuals from the nightly AFAS extract for the named cost centres, plus agency rates and the relevant CAO premiums.
Build the standard cases: base, downside, upside, and the financing alternative when a Rabobank quote or a lease is part of the request.
Flag missing inputs, any case that swings on one assumption, and any labour change that needs a CAO or works-council check.
Write a one-page note: recommendation, payback, cash effect, and the assumption that would make it wrong.
The analyst accepts the assumptions or sends the case back for the missing fact, then routes it to the Controller when it is above the threshold.
in_practice.human_gate: The FP&A analyst approves every case before anyone uses it. Above the amount the Controller sets, the Controller approves before a commitment. A case that changes shifts or headcount also goes to the HR Business Partner first.
data_needed: Twelve to twenty-four months of actuals by cost centre and site
Agency rate cards and typical invoice lag
Volume and service assumptions from the requester
in_practice.logs_to: A case register in SharePoint: request, cases, assumptions, approver, decision, and a link to the workbook.

evidence.claim: Workday Adaptive Planning, Anaplan, and Pigment run driver-based scenarios and keep versioned cases for operating plans and financing alternatives.
evidence.source: Workday Adaptive Planning, Anaplan, and Pigment; model knowledge of product scope

evidence.claim: Excel fed by a nightly ERP extract, and Power BI on that extract, are the ordinary tools finance teams use for this comparison today.
evidence.source: Microsoft Excel and Microsoft Power BI; model knowledge

evidence.claim: A gated run that fills a standard logistics case from an AFAS extract and a rate card is plausible, while the volume assumption still has to come from operations.
A large investment or a loan can fall under the works council's advice rights, so some financing cases are a consultation as well as a spreadsheet.

risks: Agency invoices, fuel, and lease quotes sit outside the nightly AFAS extract, so a case looks complete and is wrong.
A site manager takes the base case and skips the assumption that makes it positive.
A labour case recommends fewer people or a different shift pattern without the HR Business Partner or the works council.
Internal transport between Rotterdam, Tilburg, and Venlo is counted twice, and the payback is overstated.
research_questions: How many of these requests were done in the last twelve months, how many days did each take, and how many reused a workbook?
Which inputs are missing from the nightly AFAS extract, and how many days late are agency invoices, fuel, and lease costs?
What amount does the Controller already treat as needing a written case, and how many smaller requests were approved on mail alone?
Did any case in the last year change after the fact because of CAO premiums, a works-council objection, or double-counted internal flows?

tasks.short: Look for cost leaks and margin gaps across the three sites.

today.trigger: The month-close variance, a margin dip against the forecast, or a direct question from the Finance Director. The budget round starts the same search again.
steps: Scan Power BI and the AFAS actuals against budget for labour, flex, overtime, transport, and warehouse cost.
Pick a few large variances and export them to Excel.
Ask the site lead or the bookkeeper what happened, and wait.
Write a short note with one or two ideas and no named owner.
Leave most ideas there, because the next close starts.
drudgery: Clicking through the same dashboards after every refresh.
Exporting and re-pivoting so the three sites can be compared on a fair basis.
Writing variance notes that describe the gap and never name a cause.
today.time_sinks: The time goes into building a comparable view across Rotterdam, Tilburg, and Venlo, then waiting on operations for a cause. Useful ideas expire when the next close takes the following week.

lenses.faster: The monthly scan, the fair comparison across sites, and the first list of candidate leaks are ready before the analyst opens the dashboard. Choosing what is real stays with the analyst.
lenses.autonomous: After the nightly AFAS refresh, any tracked driver that crosses a threshold the analyst has set produces a short candidate with the numbers attached.
lenses.ambitious: At a tenth of the effort, Noordhaven would keep a live pipeline of small profit ideas per site, each one tested and then kept or killed, through the year and through peak season.
lenses.joy: The dashboard tour and the export are work nobody will miss. The part people value is a conversation with a site lead about a cause they recognise.
lenses.options: For each material leak, several moves arrive with a rough euro range: change the flex mix, move volume between sites, reprice a lane, change an overtime pattern, or chase a slow-paying customer group.
lenses.altitude: The analyst stops hunting variances by hand and sets the drivers, the thresholds, and the test for whether an idea is worth a site lead's time.
reach: The Controller's first-pass commentary on the flash result.
The Credit and Collections Officer's DSO bridges for the cash forecast.
The bookkeepers' view of invoice and coding errors that hide the true cost of a month.
The People Analytics analyst's site-level comparison of own staff, overtime, and agency flex per moved unit.

tasks.human_edge: The analyst can tell a real operational leak from a booking quirk, and can judge which site lead will take an idea on.
tasks.pattern_why: Ranking structured gaps on the AFAS extract is pattern work a model can prepare. Deciding what is actionable, and getting a site to own it, stays with the analyst, which matches how little of this task a model can finish alone.

in_practice.trigger: The nightly AFAS refresh lands in Power BI, or a labour, margin, or cash driver crosses a threshold the analyst has set.
steps: Compare actuals with the forecast on a fixed driver set: labour per order, flex premium, overtime, subcontracted transport, warehouse cost, and DSO.
Rank gaps by euro effect, drop anything explained by a known one-off, and keep gaps that repeated last month.
Draft a few candidate moves per material gap, each with a euro range and the extra fact that would confirm it.
The analyst removes the false ones and keeps a short list for the site lead or the Controller.
Record which ideas were accepted, measured, or killed, and feed the accepted ones into the next forecast.
in_practice.human_gate: No idea goes to a site or into the forecast until the FP&A analyst has marked it as worth a conversation. Anything that changes staffing goes through the HR Business Partner and, where the WOR requires it, the works council.
data_needed: Driver definitions agreed with the Controller
Forecast and budget by site and cost centre
Flex hours and rates, and overtime hours
in_practice.logs_to: An opportunity log the Controller can open: driver, euro range, owner, status, and whether it changed the next forecast.

evidence.claim: Power BI can hold a refreshed actual-versus-budget model and raise a threshold alert, so the monthly scan does not have to start from a blank export.
evidence.source: Microsoft Power BI; model knowledge of product scope

evidence.claim: AFAS Profit management information already shows actuals against budget for finance users, which is the feed this search starts from.
evidence.source: AFAS Profit; model knowledge of product scope

evidence.claim: Turning a variance into a profit idea that a warehouse or transport lead will own is still a conversation; the tool is better at finding the gap than at getting it accepted.

A labour idea kept at site and cost-centre level, and decided by a person, stays outside automated decisions about individual workers. Ranking named employees would be a different, and riskier, system under the EU AI Act.

risks: The list chases booking noise, and after a few false alarms the site leads stop reading it.
A labour-cost idea is sent to operations as if it were only a finance variance, without HR or the works council.
The three sites do different work, so a league table of cost per order treats unlike warehouses as the same.
An idea that was never accepted is still written into the forecast, and the business trusts the next one less.
research_questions: Of the improvement notes written in the last year, how many changed a forecast or a cost, and how many were commentary only?
Are Rotterdam, Tilburg, and Venlo comparable on the drivers we would watch, or does customer mix make a ranking misleading?
Do site leads already have a Power BI view they ignore, and what would a shortlist have to show to be used?
Which of the likely leaks sit outside the nightly extract, such as agency invoices, damage, and empty kilometres?

role.altitude: The two analysts stop assembling the monthly story by hand. They run the small system that turns the nightly AFAS extract and the board's directives into a forecast and a close pack the sites recognise, and they spend the rest of the month on the assumptions that move profit.
reach: The Controller's first-pass variance commentary and the forecast bridge at close.
The bookkeepers' patterns in invoice errors and coding that move the month's cost.
The Credit and Collections Officer's DSO bridge by customer group for the cash forecast.
The Accountants' completeness checks on accruals, leases, and agency-invoice cut-off.
The People Analytics and HRIS Analyst's site-level labour cost per unit, own staff against flex and overtime, with no personal data.
The HR Business Partner's cost side of a flex or shift proposal before it goes to the works council.
role.ceiling_note: Two people cannot sit in every site conversation, and the month still closes on a calendar. The nightly AFAS extract, late agency invoices, and the volume figures operations provide cap how fast a forecast becomes trustworthy. Labour scenarios stop at the CAO and the works council, and the swing from 150 to 300 flex workers will keep producing exceptions no rule file covers.
skills_to_grow: Driver-based forecasting in one standard model, so each new question does not start a new workbook.
SQL on the AFAS extract, so the work is not limited to the Power BI pages that exist today.
A one-page decision note a site lead will use: the recommendation, the euro effect, and the assumption that breaks it.
Enough WOR, CAO, and AVG judgment to know when a labour idea must go to HR or the works council, and when a file must stay aggregated.
A simple test for any model or agent they put in the close: what it used, what it ignored, and how to explain a number the Finance Director will challenge.
role.ambitious_version: A rolling forecast by site, cost centre, and labour type that the operations directors will staff and quote against, refreshed from the nightly extract. Every material gap is either explained or sitting with a named owner. The month closes in a few days because the surprises were already in the forecast, and the analysts spend their time on the design of that system and on the few calls that need a person in the room.
